title: Existential therapy for treating chronic pain: A scoping review
authors: Amara Kohlert; Natasha L. Gallant; Taylor G. Hill; Kelsy Dabek
fulltext_exclusion_reason: fewer than two domains substantively covered
pain_condition_detail: chronic pain (including terminal cancer, multiple sclerosis, chronic non-cancer pain, and unspecified chronic pain lasting about ten years)
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the BPS label as background framing to justify existential therapy as holistic, but does not operationalize BPS in its methods or analysis. The review scopes existential interventions and does not measure or integrate biological, psychological, and social factors.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that existential therapy may reduce pain by decreasing pain sensitivity or reducing negative evaluation of pain, linking psychological intervention to biological outcomes. No social or triadic mechanisms are proposed.
conceptual_tensions_1: Existential therapy and CBT have different theoretical underpinnings (accommodative vs. assimilative), yet the paper recommends combining them without resolving the tension
conceptual_tensions_2: Meaningfulness is central to all interventions but was not measured as an outcome in one study and not statistically significant in another, raising questions about operationalization
conceptual_tensions_3: Spirituality moderates outcomes but is not clearly distinguished from existential concerns, the paper treats them as overlapping
additional_observations_1: The paper scopes existential therapy for chronic pain but does not integrate BPS domains, it focuses almost exclusively on psychological and existential/spiritual factors
additional_observations_2: The BPS label is used only in the introduction as background framing, it does not structure the methods, results, or discussion
additional_observations_3: Social factors are virtually absent, only 'existential isolation' is mentioned, and no social determinants, support, or context are discussed
synthesis_note: This scoping review uses the BPS label as background framing to justify existential therapy as holistic, but does not operationalize BPS. It focuses on psychological and existential/spiritual factors, with minimal biological and social content. Integration is limited to directional claims linking existential therapy to pain reduction. The paper contributes to the existential therapy literature but not to BPS operationalization.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but social domain is minimal and no triadic integration occurs. Triadic integration is 'none' as domains are not related. Psych-dominant due to heavy focus on psychological and existential constructs.

context_note: Studies came from Germany, the United States, Australia, and Iran; the review excluded non-English publications.
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification
bps_operationalization_summary: The review uses BPS only to frame existential therapy as holistic and to say health is body, mind, and environment. It does not code studies by BPS domains or operationalize body/mind/environment; data are extracted as intervention/outcome themes, pain outcomes, and existential/spiritual measures.
integration_mechanism_summary: No three-domain mechanism is proposed. The paper proposes that existential or spiritual therapy may reduce pain by decreasing pain sensitivity or reducing negative evaluation of painful experiences, and that spirituality may moderate outcomes; healthcare system gaps are described as context.
emergent_labels_1: Anderson et al., Lima et al
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses BPS to justify holistic care but never operationalizes body, mind, and environment in extraction or analysis
conceptual_tensions_2: Existential or spiritual mechanisms for pain reduction are proposed through pain sensitivity and negative evaluation, but no detailed pathway is given
conceptual_tensions_3: Existentialism is treated as academically labeled, while definitions and related terms such as spiritual, humanistic, and phenomenological approaches may capture different interventions
conceptual_tensions_4: Spirituality is described as a moderator and intervention theme, but its measurement and mechanism are not specified
conceptual_tensions_5: The review includes physical functioning and pain outcomes but gives only thin social content, mainly medical system gaps, country, religion, and language
additional_observations_1: BPS is not used as a coding scheme, extraction fields are intervention details and outcomes
additional_observations_2: The review treats spirituality as a moderator of existential therapy, not as a social determinant
additional_observations_3: Included conditions are heterogeneous and mostly not musculoskeletal or neuropathic
additional_observations_4: The paper names CBT as comparator and adjunct, and suggests combined existential-CBT trials
additional_observations_5: No quality or risk-of-bias assessment is reported
synthesis_note: This review uses BPS mainly as a holistic rationale for existential/spiritual therapy, not as an operationalized model. It maps existential interventions and pain/mental-health outcomes, with pain sensitivity and negative evaluation as possible pathways and spirituality as moderator; social factors remain contextual.
coding_rationale: BPS is peripheral; biological/psychological/existential content dominate, social content thin; no triadic mechanism, so partial integration and pseudo-BPS typology.

title: Existential therapy for treating chronic pain: A scoping review
authors: Amara Kohlert; Natasha L. Gallant; Taylor G. Hill; Kelsy Dabek
pain_condition_detail: existential therapy for treating chronic pain
bps_operationalization_summary: Positions BPS as explanatory framework for understanding how existential concerns interact with physical and psychological aspects of chronic pain, without specifying mechanisms or operationalizing the model beyond describing it as an interaction between body, mind, and environment.
emergent_labels_10: combined existential, spiritual, and cognitive‐behavioral treatment method
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between BPS label usage and complete absence of social domain content
conceptual_tensions_2: Tension between claimed integration of body, mind, environment and actual focus on psychological/existential factors only
conceptual_tensions_3: Tension between theorized mechanisms (pain sensitivity reduction) and lack of specified pathways
additional_observations_1: Review focuses exclusively on existential therapy interventions, not broader BPS applications
additional_observations_2: Spirituality emerges as critical moderator not captured in standard BPS triad
additional_observations_3: CBT integration positioned as necessary complement to existential therapy for physical outcomes
additional_observations_4: All six included studies are RCTs or experimental designs, no purely qualitative BPS analyses
synthesis_note: This scoping review examines existential therapy for chronic pain through a BPS lens but demonstrates pseudo-BPS operationalization: while using the biopsychosocial label and describing interactions between body, mind, and environment, it completely omits the social domain. The review is psychologically dominant, focusing on meaning, identity, death anxiety, and acceptance as psychological constructs, with biological content limited to pain symptoms and sensitivity.
